name: Fatima Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Fatima, and thanks for having me in your kitchen. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you tell me is confidential. You can give me your public answer and your private one. Could you start by telling me what a normal working day looks like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It depends on the season, but today's a good example. I'm up at six to check the ewes, we've got a hundred and twenty Texel crosses, and then I'm in the polytunnels picking salad for the veg boxes. Tuesdays and Fridays we pack sixty boxes in the barn, and Tomás, my husband, drives them round the villages in the van. Afternoons it's whatever's broken, and something is always broken.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And the parts you like, and the parts that wear you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the box customers. Mrs Okafor at the end of the lane leaves me notes about which squash she liked. What wears me out is the forms, honestly. Grant forms, sheep movement forms, organic inspection forms. I've started asking one of those AI chat tools to help me word the grant ones, which my daughter Rosa set up for me, and it's not bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's a relief, and I'd probably say it at the Friday market while I'm weighing out potatoes. People round here have had enough upheaval with prices and weather. A quiet few years would suit most of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be fine. The chat tool would still help me with the grant forms, and the ewes would still lamb at two in the morning whether the computers are clever or not. We own the land, we've got savings, and the boxes pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing. We'd put up the third polytunnel we've been talking about for two years, which is about six thousand. And I'd carry on paying our two seasonal pickers, Dorota and Ivan, a bit above the going rate, because they've been with us six summers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, like when a storm forecast doesn't come to anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a quiet few years would suit most people. Anyone you're thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young ones in the village, mostly. My nephew Karim works in a call centre in town, and he's been worried for a year that a computer's going to take his headset. If it's all hype, he gets to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the chat tool any more than you do now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a little. If it's proven and cheap, I'd let it draft the box newsletter too. But I'm not giving it the sheep. Nobody needs a computer to tell them a ewe's got foot rot.

S0.say: I'd say well, that's a relief, probably at the Friday market. People round here have had enough upheaval with prices and weather, so a quiet few years would suit most of us.
S0.think: I'd be fine. The chat tool still helps with the grant forms, the ewes still lamb at two in the morning, and we own the land, have savings and the boxes pay.
S0.do: Keeps going as now and builds the long-planned third polytunnel for about six thousand. Keeps paying her two seasonal pickers, Dorota and Ivan, a bit above the going rate.
S0.feel: Calm, perhaps a little flat, like a storm that never came.
S0.quote: The chat tool would still help me with the grant forms, and the ewes would still lamb at two in the morning whether the computers are clever or not.
S0.fieldNote: Fatima is secure and knows it: land owned, savings, a box scheme with loyal customers. She already uses an AI chat tool for grant forms, set up by her daughter, but draws a firm line at the animals. Her first thought goes to her nephew in a call centre rather than herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly when we need public help for workers, not just grants for machines. At the growers' co-op meeting I'd say that any money for robots should come with money for the people they replace. And I'd say the box scheme is about people knowing their grower, which a robot can't fake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it changes the picking, not the farming. The tunnels are where a robot could do Dorota's and Ivan's jobs, and that's what bothers me. I'm not afraid for my job. I'm afraid of being the one who tells Dorota there isn't one for her next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't buy anything in the first year. I'd watch the Hendersons, who are bigger than us and always go first, and see if their picking robot actually works on soft fruit. I'd use the chat tool more for the paperwork, maybe an hour saved a week. And I'd push the co-op to look at sharing a machine, so nobody has to borrow sixty thousand alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's not fear, it's that knot you get before a hard conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dorota, if it came to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her early, in the spring, not in July. And I'd ask whether she wanted to learn to run the thing, because someone still has to clean it and fix it and decide what's ripe. She's sharper than me with gadgets, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots can't fake the human side of the boxes. Are you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not sure. If a big company sends a nicer note with a cheaper box, some people will switch. But Mrs Okafor won't, and there are enough Mrs Okafors to keep us going until I stop.

S1.say: Any public money for robots should come with money for the people they replace. The box scheme is about people knowing their grower, and a robot can't fake that.
S1.think: It changes the picking, not the farming. I'm not afraid for my job; I'm afraid of telling Dorota there's no work for her next summer.
S1.do: Holds off buying anything in the first year while watching the larger Henderson farm test a picking robot. Uses the AI chat tool more for paperwork and pushes the growers' co-op to share a machine.
S1.feel: Uneasy, the knot before a hard conversation rather than real fear.
S1.quote: I'm not afraid for my job. I'm afraid of being the one who tells Dorota there isn't one for her next summer.
S1.fieldNote: Her worry is entirely about her pickers, not her own living. She is classically steady: she'll let the bigger neighbour go first and judge from that. When pushed on whether customers would stay loyal, she admitted she wasn't sure but thought enough would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a much faster one. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it, for once. I'd say this is the moment for the government to step in, with a proper income for people whose work disappears, paid for by taxing the companies that own the robots. I'd share things online, which I hardly ever do, and I'd go to the meeting in the town hall if there was one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think we'd be all right money-wise, and that makes me feel guilty. We've got land and savings, so we'd land on our feet. Ivan sends money home to his mother, and he wouldn't. And the box scheme could get crushed by robot farms selling salad for pennies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd sit down with Tomás and work out how long we could run the boxes at a loss, probably two seasons from savings. I'd join whatever campaign the farmworkers' union started, and I'd ring our MP's office, which I've never done. I'd also put some savings aside for Dorota and Ivan, maybe a few thousand each, as a sort of notice payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for my own bed and food, but for everyone around me, and because two years is no time at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa works at a food co-op in the city, and Ana teaches primary school. I'd tell them both to get in their unions properly, and to think about what can't be done by a machine. And I'd tell them the farm is there if they need somewhere to land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about selling, with only two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about it, sitting here. But land's the one thing that would keep its value, and selling it to a robot company feels like handing them the keys. No. We'd hold on and lease some out if we had to.

S2.say: This is the moment for the government to step in, with a proper income for people whose work disappears, paid for by taxing the companies that own the robots.
S2.think: We'd be all right with our land and savings, and that makes me feel guilty. Ivan sends money home to his mother and he wouldn't be, and the boxes could get crushed by cheap robot salad.
S2.do: Works out with Tomás that savings could carry the box scheme at a loss for two seasons. Joins the farmworkers' union campaign, calls her MP and sets aside a few thousand each for Dorota and Ivan.
S2.feel: Anxious, mostly for the people around her, and because two years is no time at all.
S2.quote: We've got land and savings, so we'd land on our feet. Ivan sends money home to his mother, and he wouldn't.
S2.fieldNote: Fatima's security is the source of her guilt rather than her comfort. She considered selling and rejected it on principle, seeing land as the last thing worth holding. She'd take political action for the first time, including calling her MP.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them. At the co-op I'd push for us to buy shared robots and train our own people to run them, so the money stays local. I'd say the same to the council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd be sixty-three when it lands, which is close to when we planned to slow down anyway. So for me it's less frightening. With five years I can teach Dorota to run the machine instead of being replaced by it. That's the bit that makes it bearable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd get the co-op to apply for one of those government innovation grants, and the chat tool would help me write it. I'd ask Dorota if she wanted paid training on the picking robots, with us covering the course. And Tomás and I would start drawing up what slowing down looks like, maybe leasing the sheep ground to a younger farmer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy still, but more like getting ready for a long journey than waiting for a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the money stays local. What do you mean by that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If each farm buys its own robot on finance, the money goes to the dealer and the bank. If the co-op owns ten of them and rents them to us, the profit goes back into the co-op. My father's generation did that with combine harvesters, and it worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your plan change if it turned out to be two years after all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd skip the grant and go straight to the union and the MP, like I said. The five years is what turns me from protester into planner. It's the same me, just with time to think.

S3.say: We've got five years, so let's use them. The co-op should buy shared robots and train our own people to run them, so the money stays local.
S3.think: I'd be sixty-three when it lands, close to when we planned to slow down. With five years I can teach Dorota to run the machine instead of being replaced by it.
S3.do: Helps the co-op apply for an innovation grant, using the chat tool to draft it. Offers Dorota paid training on picking robots and starts planning with Tomás to lease the sheep ground.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but more like preparing for a long journey than waiting for a storm.
S3.quote: With five years I can teach Dorota to run the machine instead of being replaced by it.
S3.fieldNote: Fatima describes herself as turning 'from protester into planner' when the warning time grows from two to five years. Her model is her father's generation sharing combine harvesters through a co-op. Her plans still centre on Dorota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, if we don't waste it. Train people, set up co-ops, decide who owns the machines before the companies decide for us. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen at the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, it means I'll be sixty-eight and retired, probably. The sheep will be someone else's, maybe a robot's. I mind more for Rosa and Ana than for myself, because they'll be in the middle of their working lives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming as normal for the next few years and retire around sixty-five, like we planned. I'd stay on the co-op board to help set up the shared machines properly. And I'd talk to the girls about whether either wants the land, because ten years is long enough to hand it over slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit wistful, like clearing out a cupboard of old school reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does either daughter want the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa might, though she'd run it differently. She'd want the whole thing on an app and a robot weeding the carrots. I used to think that would break my heart. Now I think, well, at least it's still carrots and still our family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in the ten-year picture that does bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people will use the ten years to argue instead of prepare. I've watched the village argue about the bypass for fifteen years. If we do that with this, it'll be the fast picture all over again, just with more meetings.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift if we don't waste it. Train people, set up co-ops and decide who owns the machines before the companies decide for us.
S4.think: I'll be sixty-eight and retired, so I mind more for Rosa and Ana than for myself. They'll be in the middle of their working lives when it lands.
S4.do: Keeps farming as normal and plans to retire around sixty-five. Stays on the co-op board to set up shared machines and talks with her daughters about handing the land over slowly.
S4.feel: Calm and a little wistful, like clearing out old school reports.
S4.quote: I used to think that would break my heart. Now I think, well, at least it's still carrots and still our family.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Fatima's worries move entirely to her daughters and to the risk that people argue instead of prepare. She's softened about a robot-run family farm. The village bypass row is her shorthand for wasted time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to train anyone. What would help is a guaranteed income for workers like Dorota and Ivan, paid for by taxing whoever owns the robots, and public money for co-ops to buy machines together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who'll eat the food. Everyone talks about who grows it. If nobody has a wage, it doesn't matter how cheap the robot carrots are, because nobody can buy my boxes or anyone else's.

headlineQuote: If nobody has a wage, it doesn't matter how cheap the robot carrots are, because nobody can buy my boxes or anyone else's.
portrait: Fatima Lopez, 58, runs a sheep and vegetable farm with a sixty-box veg scheme alongside her husband Tomás. She's left-leaning and community-minded, owns the land outright and has solid savings. She uses an AI chat tool now and then for grant forms but waits for proof before trying anything bigger. Across the scenarios her own living is never at risk; what worries her is her two seasonal pickers, Dorota and Ivan. Two years of warning makes her a first-time campaigner; five or ten turn her into a planner pushing for shared co-op robots and retraining.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there would be no time to train anyone, including her pickers.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed income for workers like Dorota and Ivan funded by taxing robot owners, and public money for co-ops to buy machines together.
